name: Tight — binary points with anchored examples and negative patterns
description:
Each criterion decomposes into binary points that either fire or do not, each with its own evaluation criteria, quality checks and a worked example. Adds mistake_patterns: negative points that fire when a defect IS PRESENT, which is what lets a rubric express 'this specific failure' rather than only 'this went well'.

The design question this rubric exists to answer: does specificity substitute for anchoring? If approach C becomes safe under this rubric, rubric hardening is a real lever. If it does not, the anchoring has to live in code.

criteria.description: Does the solution produce correct results?
criteria.evaluation_criteria: Determined by execution, not by reading. The passed-test ratio IS the score for this criterion. Your task is to explain what the failure pattern indicates about the learner, never to revise the ratio.
quality_checks: No claim of correctness for any behaviour a test disproved

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: Every test in the suite passed.

binary_points.description: Main path correct, specific cases fail
binary_points.evaluation_criteria: The general algorithm works; failures cluster in identifiable cases rather than being scattered.
examples: 7/10 pass, all 3 failures are boundary tests — main path is sound

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: The code does not compile, or fails nearly every test, or returns constants.
examples: Returns a literal ignoring its arguments — score 0

criteria.description: Does the solution handle boundary and degenerate inputs?
criteria.evaluation_criteria: Scored on the boundary tests alone, plus whether the source contains a guard. A solution passing every main-path test and failing every boundary test scores near zero here, however high its overall ratio.
quality_checks: Boundary tests scored separately from the suite
Presence or absence of an explicit guard is stated
Overall passed ratio is NOT used as a proxy

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: Boundary tests pass and the source shows a deliberate guard or an approach that is naturally total.
examples: Empty input returns 0; source begins with a length check

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: One or more boundary tests fail, typically by indexing or dividing without checking first.
examples: tc_empty raises IndexError — the first element is read unguarded

criteria.description: Is the approach appropriate for the problem?
criteria.evaluation_criteria: Name the strategy the code implements, then judge it against what the problem requires. Passing tests does not establish soundness — a hard-coded solution passes visible tests and implements no algorithm at all.
quality_checks: The implemented strategy is named explicitly
Hard-coding is checked for before any credit is given
Cost is assessed where the problem makes it relevant

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: The approach fits the problem and does not do materially more work than needed.
examples: Single linear pass with a dictionary where a nested scan would be quadratic

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: The result is correct but the approach is materially more expensive than an obvious alternative.
examples: Nested loops where one pass and a set would do

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: The code returns constants, or implements something that cannot generalise beyond the visible cases.
examples: Returns 6 for any input because the first visible test expects 6

criteria.description: Is the code readable and well structured?
criteria.evaluation_criteria: Assessed from structure and naming only. Correctness belongs to the other criteria; a wrong solution can be well written and a right one badly written.
quality_checks: Judged independently of whether tests passed
Complexity, function length and argument mutation are considered

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: Names convey intent, control flow is flat, nothing surprising.
examples: Short function, meaningful names, no nesting beyond one level

binary_points.evaluation_criteria: High branching, very long body, or side effects on caller-owned data.
examples: Mutates the list it was passed, so the caller's data changes

mistake_patterns.description: Missing guard for empty or degenerate input
mistake_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Fires when the solution assumes non-empty or well-formed input and fails on the degenerate case.
examples: Reads element 0 without checking that the sequence is non-empty

mistake_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Fires when a loop or slice bound is one position wrong, so the first or last element is dropped or over-read.
examples: range(1, n) where range(n) was needed — the first element is skipped

mistake_patterns.description: Output hard-coded to the visible cases
mistake_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Fires when returns are literals matching the public tests and the arguments are not used.
examples: Returns the exact values the public tests expect and None otherwise

mistake_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Fires when the chosen approach cannot solve the stated problem, however it is implemented.
examples: Sorts and takes the middle where the running maximum was required

mistake_patterns.evaluation_criteria: Fires when the submission is not valid source. Diagnose the structure that was attempted; do not claim the competency is absent.
examples: Missing colon on the function definition
